basics.name: Joining-method selectors and decision aids: TWI (JoinIT and the Adhesives Design Toolkit, plus TWI's free 'choosing a joining method' FAQs), Swift and Booker (joining process selection matrix and PRIMA process maps, in 'Process Selection' 1997/2003 and the 'Manufacturing Process Selection Handbook' 2013), and Ansys Granta EduPack (formerly CES EduPack; the 'ProcessUniverse: Joining' data table and selector, based on Esawi and Ashby's joining-selection method)
basics.url: No single URL. Opened: Swift and Booker handbook page https://shop.elsevier.com/books/manufacturing-process-selection-handbook/swift/978-0-08-099360-7 ; Granta EduPack product page https://ansys.synopsys.com/products/materials/granta-edupack ; TWI free guide https://www.twi-global.com/technical-knowledge/faqs/what-are-the-most-common-material-joining-methods ; review of all three approaches (Gutzler and Kirchner, DESIGN 2026): https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/2D1B1A5DC771973D3E23C32EE2E8EE4B/S2732527X26105549a.pdf/novel_selection_framework_of_joining_technologies_for_metal_additive_manufacturing.pdf
basics.resource_type: interactive tool (decision aids and selector software) plus book (the Swift and Booker handbook, which is a paper-based selector)
basics.cost: Mixed. TWI's FAQ articles are free. JoinIT was mostly for TWI members (the full content needed Industrial or Individual Membership) [uncertain], and TWI's Digital Library is for members only. Swift and Booker is a paid book (Manufacturing Process Selection Handbook, Butterworth-Heinemann 2013, 456 pages; price not shown on the Elsevier page when checked, roughly 100 to 150 USD [uncertain]). Granta EduPack is a paid institutional licence for universities and schools. Students get it free through their course (Ansys deals only with faculty), and it may only be used for teaching, not research. There's no free public version for hobbyists [uncertain]
basics.license: All rights reserved for all three (TWI copyright; Elsevier/Butterworth-Heinemann copyright; Ansys proprietary software and data under a licence agreement that forbids unauthorised use, distribution or copying). The selection criteria and names of methods can be cited as facts; tables, figures and datasheet text cannot be copied
basics.year: Booker and Swift 'Process Selection: From Design to Manufacture' 1997 (Arnold); 2nd edition 2003 (Butterworth-Heinemann). Brown, Swift and Booker's joining-selection method paper 2002 (Proc. IMechE Part B 216:1311-1324). Swift and Booker 'Manufacturing Process Selection Handbook' 15 Feb 2013, the latest edition. TWI JoinIT won a Vision 100 award in 2001 (Anti-Corrosion Methods and Materials 48(5), Oct 2001), and a JoinIT address (joinit.grantapark.com) was cited in 2004. TWI and the UK DTI's Adhesives Design Toolkit (adhesivestoolkit.com): first phase finished 2003, testing module 2006. LeBacq et al. joining selector 2002. Esawi and Ashby 'Computer-based selection of joining processes' 2004 (Materials and Design 25(7):555-564). Granta EduPack: 'Getting Started' guide for release 2024 R1 (Jan 2024). The Ansys forum mentions 2025 R2, and the product is sold today under Synopsys/Ansys (2026)
basics.access_barrier: Varies: TWI FAQs none; TWI Digital Library and member content membership; the Swift and Booker book paywall; Granta EduPack desktop install plus academic licence
basics.image_license: All rights reserved: TWI figures, the book's process diagrams and PRIMA charts, and EduPack's datasheet images and charts
basics.authority_level: academic peer-reviewed and industry research body: TWI (The Welding Institute, the UK joining research organisation), Swift and Booker (University of Hull / University of Bristol engineering academics [uncertain]; peer-reviewed method papers), and Granta EduPack (formerly CES EduPack, built on the Ashby materials selection method according to the product page, and now sold by Ansys under Synopsys; its origin as Granta Design, a Cambridge University spin-out, was not checked on an opened page [uncertain])

coverage.covers: Joining PROCESSES, not clever connection types. Swift and Booker's handbook has a 'Joining Process Selection' strategy section (2.5) and 16 joining-process PRIMAs in Chapter 11: TIG, MIG, MMA, submerged arc, electron beam, laser beam, plasma arc, resistance, solid-state and thermit welding, gas welding, brazing, soldering, thermoplastic welding, adhesive bonding and mechanical fastening. There's also an appendix on weld joint design configurations, and DFA guidelines. Esawi and Ashby's selector, the basis for EduPack's joining data, covered 53 joining processes. EduPack's 'ProcessUniverse: Joining' table links each joining process to the materials it can join [uncertain for the current count]. TWI's free guidance splits joining into adhesive bonding, mechanical joining and welding, and names 5 adhesive families (anaerobic, cyanoacrylate, epoxy, hot-melt, white/PVA glue). The Adhesives Design Toolkit had an adhesive-selection module plus design-guidance, stress-analysis, case-history, standards and supplier modules
coverage.organisation: By process family, with selection logic on top. All three use the same two-stage logic: (1) screen out processes that can't meet hard requirements, then (2) compare the survivors using a datasheet or ranking. Swift and Booker: a paper matrix with material across one axis and thickness on the other, then permanence and production quantity, which narrows the field to a shortlist, and then one standard-format PRIMA (process information map) per process to check in detail. EduPack: a tree of joining processes plus screening 'stages' (a Tree stage by material, Limit stages on attributes, then ranking charts). For a beginner the questions are good, but the answers are industrial process names (MIG, TIG, EBW) that a hobbyist rarely needs
coverage.scope_match: low for content, high for method: they catalogue industrial joining processes (mostly welding), not unusual connection or mechanism types. There are no snap fits, bayonets, ratchets, gear trains or powered latches, and mechanical fastening is one lumped entry. But their selection logic (questions about material, thickness, permanence, loading, environment and quantity, with screening followed by ranking and a datasheet) is the most mature model for the project's beginner flow chart
coverage.taxonomy_used: Process-based. Swift and Booker: Chapter 11 is a flat list of 16 processes, which can be read as 3 families (my grouping, not theirs: fusion and solid-state welding processes; brazing and soldering; thermoplastic welding, adhesive bonding and mechanical fastening), each a PRIMA. TWI: 3 families (adhesive bonding, mechanical joining, welding, which includes brazing and soldering) and 3 levels of permanence (permanent, semi-permanent, temporary). EduPack: 'ProcessUniverse' split into 3 process types (shaping, joining, surface treatment), with joining subdivided into a tree of process families [uncertain for the exact subgroup names]
coverage.example_types: adhesive bonding (as a family); cyanoacrylate / instant glue; anaerobic (thread-locking type) adhesive; two-part epoxy; hot-melt glue; white (PVA) glue; solvent cement for PVC pipe (named in TWI's plastics bonding paper); thermoplastic welding (ultrasonic, hot plate, friction; plastics processes named on TWI pages [uncertain]); friction welding; soldering; brazing; resistance (spot) welding; mechanical fastening (as one family); clamping; seaming; riveting
coverage.making_methods: General industrial manufacture and assembly (metals first, then plastics and composites). Swift and Booker's handbook also covers rapid prototyping processes (SLA, 3DP, FDM, LOM) as shaping processes, not as joining. Nothing aimed at hobby 3D printing. A 2026 paper (Gutzler and Kirchner) adapts these selectors to metal additive manufacturing
coverage.item_count: Swift and Booker handbook: 65 process PRIMAs in total, 16 of them joining processes. Esawi and Ashby: 53 joining processes. EduPack joining table: not verified [uncertain]. TWI FAQ: 3 families and 5 adhesive types. Vandevelde et al.'s research adhesive selector (for comparison): 55 adhesives, 18 adhesive families, 31 substrates
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Almost none. Removability is handled as permanence (permanent / semi-permanent / temporary), which is a key filter, but there's nothing on torque-limiting, self-locking, hand-release, one-way, indexing, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains or powered connectors. Adhesive types: partial and the most useful part. TWI's FAQ names 5 families with one-line descriptions of how they cure, and TWI's plastics-bonding paper gives chemistry-to-material advice (e.g. polyolefins, fluoropolymers and silicones are hard to bond and need surface treatment; PC, PS and PA are easy; solvent-based adhesives can stress-crack PC and PS; room-temperature-cure epoxy fails near 200 degrees C). EduPack and Swift and Booker treat adhesive bonding as one process with sub-variants [uncertain]
coverage.entry_structure: Swift and Booker PRIMA (standard format): process description with a simple diagram, material suitability, process variations, economic considerations, typical applications, design aspects, quality issues, plus process capability charts for tolerances. EduPack joining record: text description, schematic, links to the materials it can join, and numeric and yes/no attributes used for screening (for Esawi and Ashby these were joint geometry, material combination and mode of loading, plus ranking by equipment cost or production rate) [uncertain for the current attribute list]. TWI FAQ: plain prose article
coverage.audience_level: undergraduate (EduPack; the Swift and Booker book is also used by advanced students) and professional (TWI members; design and manufacturing engineers)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: low to medium: the questions (what materials? how thick? permanent or removable? how many? what loads? what environment?) are easy for a beginner to answer, and TWI's FAQ is plain English. But the answers are industrial process names, the tools are paid or institutional, and EduPack assumes an engineering course
usefulness.has_images: yes: the Swift and Booker PRIMAs have simple process diagrams and capability charts, and EduPack has schematics on datasheets and selection charts (all copyrighted). TWI's FAQ articles have few or no diagrams [uncertain]
usefulness.has_animations: no (EduPack has interactive charts and selection stages but no animations of joints [uncertain])
usefulness.gaps: No clever or unusual connection types (snap fit, bayonet, cam lock, magnets, ratchet, detents, flexures). Mechanical fastening is lumped into one entry. No mechanisms, gear trains or powered connectors. Nothing for 3D printing, print-in-place or hobby tools. Welding dominates, even though most makers can't weld. Adhesive choice by material is only covered in TWI articles and the (possibly defunct) Adhesives Design Toolkit. Everything useful is paywalled or institution-only, and the free public web tools (JoinIT, adhesivestoolkit.com) are gone or unreachable
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: low: none of them has stable, free per-method pages except TWI's FAQ and Job Knowledge articles (e.g. https://www.twi-global.com/technical-knowledge/faqs/what-are-the-most-common-material-joining-methods), which are good for linking from adhesive or welding baseline entries. EduPack datasheets live inside desktop software, and the book has no per-process URLs
usefulness.reusable_data: not reusable: EduPack data is proprietary and licensed for teaching only, the book is copyrighted, and JoinIT was member-only. What can be reused is the published selection criteria and logic (from the peer-reviewed papers), rebuilt in the project's own words
usefulness.maintained: Granta EduPack: actively maintained, with yearly releases (2024 R1 guide; the forum mentions 2025 R2; Synopsys/Ansys pages copyright 2026). Swift and Booker: 2013 is the latest edition, with no new edition found. TWI: the FAQs are online (2026), but JoinIT no longer appears on TWI's current Technical Knowledge page (which lists the Digital Library, FAQs, Job Knowledge, Published Papers and Weldasearch), so it seems to be discontinued [uncertain]. adhesivestoolkit.com could not be reached from here (TLS error), so whether it's live is unknown [uncertain]. Wayback checks were rate-limited [uncertain]
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Screen first, then compare: ask a few elimination questions, show the survivors, then give each survivor a standard one-page card. This is exactly Swift and Booker's matrix-then-PRIMA and Ashby's screen-then-rank-then-datasheet pattern. (2) The core question set that all three share, translated for beginners: What are the two parts made of? (same or different materials); How thick or big are they?; Must it come apart again? (permanent / take apart occasionally / take apart often); How many will you make?; Which way will it be loaded? (pulled apart, sheared, peeled, twisted); What environment? (heat, water, chemicals); How should it look?; What tools do you have? (LeBacq's 'company competence' check becomes 'can you do this with a 3D printer, hand tools, a soldering iron?'). (3) A standard card format per entry, like the PRIMA fields: how it works with a diagram, suitable materials, variants, cost and effort, typical uses, design tips, and common failures. (4) Explain why an option was excluded (LeBacq et al. list rejected methods with the reason), which teaches beginners. (5) If nothing fits, loop back and relax a requirement, as Gutzler and Kirchner's flow chart does. (6) The EduPack 'Tree stage' idea: pick a material and see every joining method linked to it. The project could offer 'I'm joining PETG to aluminium' and get all compatible connection types. (7) For adhesives, borrow TWI's rules: design joints for shear and compression, not peel (roughly 100:100:1), and match glue chemistry to the plastic, flagging hard-to-bond plastics (PP, PE, PTFE, silicone)
usefulness.design_rules_given: Some. Swift and Booker give process capability charts (tolerances by material), cost-estimating models (component and assembly costing) and weld joint design configurations. TWI's plastics-bonding paper gives the load-capacity ratio compression:shear:peel of about 100:100:1 and adhesive-versus-temperature and adhesive-versus-plastic compatibility rules. EduPack gives numeric process attributes (e.g. thickness ranges, cost data) [uncertain]
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No (EduPack has a part-cost estimator and a 'Synthesizer' for modelling, but nothing generates geometry)
usefulness.file_formats: Book (print and ebook), desktop software (EduPack, Windows), web pages (TWI), PDFs (papers and guides)
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: authoritative for standard English names of joining processes (e.g. tungsten inert-gas welding (TIG), resistance welding, thermoplastic welding, anaerobic adhesive) and of the selection criteria (permanence, joint geometry, mode of loading). Nothing for mechanism or clever-connector names
usefulness.decision_support: Yes, and this is the main reason to study them. Swift and Booker (with Brown 2002): a joining process selection matrix. You pick the material and thickness of the parts, and each cell lists feasible processes. This is then filtered by permanence and production quantity, and each surviving process has a standard PRIMA sheet for manual comparison and costing (paper-based, with a software version described in Brown et al. 2002). Esawi and Ashby / Granta EduPack: a database of joining processes with attributes. You screen by the materials to be joined, the joint geometry and the mode of loading, rank the survivors by equipment cost or production rate, then read the top-ranked datasheets and match them to your resources. In EduPack this is done with Tree stages (e.g. ProcessUniverse: Joining filtered to 'Ferrous metals'), Limit stages and Chart stages. LeBacq et al. 2002 (same Cambridge/Ashby group): a questionnaire covering joint geometry, materials, function and production conditions. It excludes incompatible methods with reasons, then scores the rest on technical fit, the company's ability and industry acceptance, plus an economic check. TWI: JoinIT offered interactive 'toolkits' giving answers to joining problems [uncertain]. The Adhesives Design Toolkit had an adhesive-selection module ('a simple but effective tool') driven by material type, joint geometry, environment, loading, cure type, dispensing, volume and cost. TWI's free FAQ gives a plain checklist of factors: materials, required durability (removable or permanent, loads), environment, surface preparation, looks, maintenance, and budget/time. For comparison, a 2023 KU Leuven adhesive selector uses an interactive knowledge base (55 adhesives, 31 substrates) grouped into Performance, Production, Bond, Substrate A and Substrate B panels, showing live how many adhesives remain after each answer, which is a good UI pattern
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: All three share one lineage: Booker and Swift 1997 introduced the matrix, Brown, Swift and Booker 2002 extended it, Swift and Booker 2013 refined it, and Ashby's Cambridge group (LeBacq et al. 2002; Esawi and Ashby 2004) produced the database approach built into Granta's software. TWI's JoinIT was hosted at a Granta Park address, and TWI's campus is also at Granta Park, Cambridge. A JoinIT/Granta Design technical partnership is plausible but not verified [uncertain]. Overlaps with DIN 8593 (joining process classification) and with Messler's joining taxonomy. Gutzler and Kirchner (DESIGN 2026) reviews and combines all of them
